cleanIntro: The K 95 is a BREAK-ACTION SINGLE SHOT with a removable breech block, and its safety is not a safety at all — it is a COCKING slide. The firing pin spring sits uncocked until you push the slide forward, which means the rifle is mechanically at rest whenever the slide is back. ⛔ Blaser warns twice about this rifle in ways that matter here: never put a finger in the trigger guard while UNCOCKING it, and the direct-pull trigger's pull weight may only be changed at the factory.

steps.title: ⛔ The slide is a COCKING slide — back is at rest, forward is armed
steps.action: Blaser's safety system on the K 95 works on an UNCOCKED firing pin spring: the spring is not under load until the safety slide (cocking slide) is pushed forward, immediately before the shot. ⚠ So a slide that is back means the striker spring is down, not merely that a block is in the way.
steps.prose: This is the opposite of a conventional safety, and it is why the rifle can be stored with nothing under tension.
steps.quote: The safety system of the Blaser K 95 is based on an uncocked firing pin spring. The firing pin spring is cocked with the safety slide (cocking slide) immediately before the shot.
steps.cite: BLASER K 95 — INSTRUCTION MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code is printed in the document — 4. Safety system

steps.title: ⛔ FINGERS OUT of the trigger guard while you uncock
steps.action: To return to safe, pull the cocking slide back with your THUMB against a light resistance and let it run back. ⛔ Blaser's CAUTION is explicit and it names the habit it is warning against: do not put your fingers on the trigger while uncocking, as you might on a rifle with an exposed hammer. On a loaded K 95 that fires the gun.
steps.prose: A warning written against a specific muscle memory is worth reading twice.
steps.aside: Simply pull safety slide (cocking slide) backwards with your thumb against a light resistance, and let it slide backwards.
steps.quote: CAUTION: Under no circumstances should you put your fingers into the trigger when locking (uncocking) your rifle (you may be used to do this from rifles with exposed hammers). This would trigger a shot, when the rifle is loaded!
steps.cite: BLASER K 95 — INSTRUCTION MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code is printed in the document — 4.2. Returning to the safe position

steps.title: Open it — and the slide safes ITSELF
steps.action: Press the locking lever all the way right and hold it, then break the barrel down. The extractor pulls the cartridge far enough out of the chamber to be taken by hand. ⚠ Blaser notes that pushing the locking lever right makes the cocking slide jump back to uncocked on its own — useful, and not a substitute for looking in the chamber.
steps.prose: A rifle that safes itself as it opens is still a rifle you look into.
steps.aside: NOTE: When opening the rifle - pressing the locking lever to the right - the safety slide (cocking slide) jumps back into the "safe” (uncocked) position automatically.
steps.quote: When breaking the barrel, the cartridge is pulled out by the extractor far enough to be taken out fully by hand.
steps.cite: BLASER K 95 — INSTRUCTION MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code is printed in the document — 7.1. Unloading the Rifle

steps.title: ⛔ Unload BEFORE disassembly — Blaser's own CAUTION
steps.action: The disassembly chapter opens with it. Unload the rifle before anything comes apart, and confirm the chamber by eye rather than by the position of the cocking slide.
steps.prose: Short sentence, first line of the chapter. That placement is the point.
steps.quote: CAUTION: Unload your rifle before disassembly (refer to page 9).
steps.cite: BLASER K 95 — INSTRUCTION MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code is printed in the document — 2. Disassembly of the Rifle — CAUTION

steps.title: Buttstock on the thigh, then the forearm flap
steps.action: Support the rifle at the buttstock on your thigh. Pull the FOREARM FLAP out with a finger of one hand and press the forearm off the barrel with the fingers of the other, then tilt it away at a slight angle and lift it off the hinge.
steps.prose: Two hands doing different jobs at once. The thigh is the third hand.
steps.caution: Support the rifle at the buttstock on your thigh.
steps.aside: Tilt forearm away from barrel at a slight angle and pull it up, removing it from the hinge.
steps.quote: Pull forearm flap out with a finger of one hand, and disengage forearm from the barrel by pressing with the fingers of your other hand.
steps.cite: BLASER K 95 — INSTRUCTION MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code is printed in the document — 2.1. Removing the forearm

steps.title: ⛔ The barrel comes off ONLY with the forearm already off
steps.action: Blaser prints the precondition as a heading of its own. With the forearm removed, press the locking lever fully right and hold it, then tilt the barrel all the way down — that is what disengages the barrel hook.
steps.prose: All the way down, not part-way. The hook releases at the end of the travel.
steps.aside: Tilt barrel all the way down. Doing so, the barrel hook is disengaged.
steps.cite: BLASER K 95 — INSTRUCTION MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code is printed in the document — 2.2. Removing the barrel
steps.warn: Press locking lever all the way to the right and hold it in this position.

steps.title: ⚠ The breech block comes out for a THOROUGH clean — or to disable the rifle
steps.action: Blaser states when this step applies: a thorough clean, or safeguarding the rifle against unauthorised use by taking the block out. Press the BLOCK LOCK beside the trigger and hold it down, press the locking lever right at the same time until the block disengages, and take it out from the FRONT — it snaps forward a little as it releases.
steps.prose: A single-shot rifle whose breech block lives in a different drawer is a genuinely inert object.
steps.aside: Press block lock 10 , located beside the trigger, and keep it pressed down.
steps.quote: This is only necessary, when you want to thoroughly clean the rifle or safeguard it against unauthorised use by removing the breech block.
steps.cite: BLASER K 95 — INSTRUCTION MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code is printed in the document — 2.3. Removing breech block
steps.warn: Now press the locking lever simultaneously to the right, until breech block disengages.

steps.title: That is the strip — barrel, forearm, breech block
steps.action: The K 95 comes apart into the barrel, the forearm and (when wanted) the breech block. Blaser publishes nothing beyond that for the owner. ⛔ The trigger in particular is a factory item on this rifle.
steps.prose: Three parts and a receiver. Clean it as what it is.
steps.quote: When disengaging, the block snaps forward a little and can now be removed, accessing it from the front.
steps.cite: BLASER K 95 — INSTRUCTION MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code is printed in the document — 2.3. Removing breech block

deepSteps.title: ⛔ The trigger pull is a FACTORY setting — not a bench adjustment
deepSteps.action: The K 95 has a DIRECT PULL trigger and Blaser's caution is absolute: the setting of the trigger pull can and may only be changed at the factory. ⚠ What the owner IS asked to do is check it regularly for smooth movement, unloaded and uncocked — gummy oil and contamination are the named causes of malfunction.
deepSteps.prose: Check it, don't set it. Those are two different jobs and only one is yours.
deepSteps.aside: NOTE: Please check the trigger regularly for smooth movement, with the rifle unloaded and locked (uncocked). Gummy oil and/or contaminations may affect proper functioning of the trigger and cause malfunctions.
deepSteps.quote: CAUTION: The Blaser K 95 is equipped with a direct pull trigger. The setting of the trigger pull can and may only be changed at the factory.
deepSteps.cite: BLASER K 95 — INSTRUCTION MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code is printed in the document — 6.1. Firing — CAUTION

deepSteps.title: ⚠ The breech block has ONE correct attitude, and vertical is not it
deepSteps.action: Blaser prints this caution twice. The breech block must sit SLIGHTLY INCLINED FORWARD; if it has gone vertical the rifle cannot be closed at all. The cure is to press the locking lever fully right and return the block to the inclined position by hand — not to force the barrel shut.
deepSteps.prose: A rifle that will not close is telling you something specific here, and it is not that the hinge is dirty.
deepSteps.aside: Put breech block with the semicircular shaft bearing 15 onto the shaft in the bottom of the receiver and tilt it backwards.
deepSteps.quote: CAUTION: The breech block must be in its slightly inclined forward position. If in a vertical position, the rifle cannot be closed any more.
deepSteps.cite: BLASER K 95 — INSTRUCTION MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code is printed in the document — 3.2. Closing the rifle — CAUTION

deepSteps.title: The closing check is a PRESSURE test, not a look
deepSteps.action: To confirm the locking lever is closed, apply light pressure to the LEFT. Blaser adds the reason: if it is not properly closed the rifle cannot be cocked, by design. ⚠ On a new rifle real force is needed to close it — the fits are tight and the wedge pulls.
deepSteps.prose: A safety interlock you can feel is better than one you have to remember.
deepSteps.aside: Mainly in new rifles, some force has to be exerted in order to close the locking lever. This is due to the tight, precise fits.
deepSteps.quote: To check whether the locking lever is closed, apply light pressure to the left. Otherwise, disengaging from safe position (cocking) of the rifle will not be possible, for safety reasons.
deepSteps.cite: BLASER K 95 — INSTRUCTION MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code is printed in the document — 3.2. Closing the rifle

deepSteps.title: ⚠ Putting the barrel back takes SKILL — Blaser says so in print
deepSteps.action: The manual asks the owner to have the barrel-securing procedure demonstrated by an expert and practised several times in his presence, and tells him not to use force. ⛔ That is unusual candour from a maker and it is worth taking at face value the first few times.
deepSteps.prose: A tight, precise fit is the whole reason this rifle shoots. It is also why it goes back together slowly.
deepSteps.quote: NOTE: Securing the barrel requires a certain amount of skill. Do not use force! We suggest having this procedure demonstrated by an expert and practise several times in his presence.
deepSteps.cite: BLASER K 95 — INSTRUCTION MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code is printed in the document — 1.2. Assembling the rifle — NOTE

deepSteps.title: ⛔ Oil in the action can HARDEN
deepSteps.action: When oiling, keep oil and grease out of the trigger and action system: Blaser states it can resinify — harden — and cause dangerous malfunctions. ⚠ Metal parts DO want a light oil, and the wooden stock wants stock care products and not gun oil.
deepSteps.prose: Three different surfaces, three different products, and the action wants none of them.
deepSteps.aside: Metal parts: Keep all metal parts of the rifle clean and slightly oiled at all times.
deepSteps.quote: CAUTION: When oiling hunting rifles, care has to be taken that no oil or grease gets into the trigger and action system. Under certain conditions, oil and grease can resinify (harden), causing dangerous disruptions of functioning.
deepSteps.cite: BLASER K 95 — INSTRUCTION MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code is printed in the document — Care and maintenance — CAUTION
deepSteps.warn: Stock preservative is not suitable for polishing metal parts!

deepSteps.title: Barrel care — after shooting AND after carrying
deepSteps.action: Blaser asks for the chamber and bore to be polished with a suitable gun oil after shooting, before long storage, and after CARRYING the rifle — especially in humid or wet conditions. ⚠ Carrying is on that list deliberately; a rifle that has not been fired can still come home wet.
deepSteps.prose: Most barrel damage on a hunting rifle happens on days it was never fired.
deepSteps.aside: Stocks: All wooden stocks of Blaser hunting rifles are oil-rubbed. We recommend to polish them regularly with standard stock care products.
deepSteps.quote: Barrel: Polish exterior and interior of chamber and barrel with a suitable gun oil after shooting, before storing the rifle for prolonged periods of time, and after carrying the rifle, especially in humid or wet conditions.
deepSteps.cite: BLASER K 95 — INSTRUCTION MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code is printed in the document — Care and maintenance — barrel
deepSteps.warn: Gun oil is not suitable for stock care!

cleaning.name: BARREL AND CHAMBER
tasks: Bore and chamber polished with gun oil after shooting
Barrel wiped free of oil before the next shot
Extra care after carrying the rifle in damp or wet weather

cleaning.name: BREECH BLOCK AND RECEIVER
tasks: Block and its shaft bearing cleaned and lightly oiled
Block lock beside the trigger checked for free movement
⛔ No oil into the trigger and action system — it can resinify

cleaning.name: METAL AND STOCK
tasks: Metal parts kept clean and slightly oiled — ⛔ NOT with stock preservative
Oil-rubbed wooden stocks polished with stock care products
⛔ Gun oil is not stock care and stock oil is not metal care

reassembly: Breech block onto the shaft in the bottom of the receiver by its semicircular bearing, then tilted back.
Block lock held down while the locking lever goes fully right, then the block re-engaged and pressed down at its rear.
Extractor pulled fully out to its stop — ⛔ do NOT touch the locking lever here.
Front barrel hook onto the hinge bolt: a tight fit, and it wants care rather than force.
Forearm engaged on the hinge bolt flush with the receiver, tilted onto the barrel and its flap closed completely.
fncheck: With the rifle confirmed unloaded, close it and check the locking lever by applying light pressure to the LEFT — Blaser's own test, and it matters because a lever that is not closed will not let the rifle cock at all. ⚠ On a new rifle expect real force to close that lever: the fits are tight and the wedge pulls. Then cock and uncock the slide a few times with your thumb, fingers well clear of the trigger guard, and confirm the trigger moves smoothly with the rifle unloaded and uncocked.
